chapter: Day jobs and Bay Area gigs
title: Swing playing, retirement, and Ben Watkins-era colleagues
summary: He played only swing from 1930 on; retired six years ago; recalls playing with Jerome Richardson and others.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Yeah. That's Alcorn. How do you spell it? A-L-C-R-N? Yeah. So now you're pretty much, though, in those days, a swing trumpet player. I mean, you were playing kind of with big bands. This was a lot different than what you grew up, the style you played in New Orleans. Yeah.
I had stopped playing the traditional jazz back in about 19. In fact, I didn't get a chance to play too much traditional jazz. Most of mine came in with Louis Armstrong and his new style of playing.
And I started back in doing that time. And from the 30s on, I did have a chance to play a little bit of the traditional jazz. But from the 30s on, from 1930 on, I played nothing but swing.
What kind of swing jazz, you're right. Yeah.
I was playing the swing numbers.
Yeah. So let's just bring it up to the present here. I guess you retired from Caterpillar how many years ago?
We're doing this interview on, what, October 6th, 1984. So you retired six years ago. But you're still playing, George.

Oh, something else I would like to add to that. Doing those years with Ben Watkins, I also played with Jerome Richardson, which is one of the world's great alto players. And I have a picture of he and I at a jam session together. And it was Ernie Lewis. He'd become one of the executives for the Musicians' Union. And Wilbur Barranco, the late Wilbur Barranco. And Vernon Alley. All these guys I used to play with.
